worlds.title: The Buttressed World, Where Only Children Stand Alone
worlds.text:
The Buttressed World, Where Only Children Stand Alone

1. The core principle

In this world, weight never presses straight down. Every bit of matter presses on whatever lies beneath it downward and outward at the same time, the way the foot of an arch presses against its pier. Deep inside a mass, these outward pushes meet one another and cancel. At any surface steeper than its material can bear, though, the pushes behind it point into open air. Only the thin press of that air meets them, so the thing spreads. Its foot creeps outward and its top sinks until its sides are gentle enough that every push lands on matter again. That slope, the repose, is the steepest shape anything can keep on its own.

So nothing holds itself up. A wall, a tower, a tree or a standing body exists only because something presses back on it where it would spread. That something is held in turn, down an unbroken chain of contact that ends in the Ground: the flat, endless floor of the world, already at repose and so the one thing that leans on nothing. The only strength there is, is the strength of a buttress. Solidity is a relation, not a property. A wall is solid because of what leans against it, and every steep thing is a claim on its neighbors.

Left alone, the world relaxes into gentle mounds. Mountains are broad domes, and any steep face in a landscape means something is holding it. Tall cliffs survive only as hollow coves whose curved faces arch sideways into their flanks, and caves are always round. Forests are shaped like hills. The tallest trees stand in the middle, leaning crown to crown on flared plank roots, and the lowest, stoutest ones stand at the rim, so a forest cut at its edge dies inward. Large land animals are either low and dome-backed or live in packed herds, and predators hunt by pushing one animal out of the press. The tallest living things grow under deep water, which presses back harder than air.

2. The rules

R1 — Steepness pushes. Any face steeper than its material's repose pushes outward. The push at each point grows with the weight above it, so the total push on a steep face grows with the square of its height: double a wall's height and it needs four times the holding. Repose is a material's defining number. Loose earth reposes at one up for two across, fitted angular stone at one for one, and water and air at none. The surroundings press back on every face. Air presses lightly and evenly, enough to answer any face down to a depth of about a grown person's hip height below its top (the Hold), and no deeper. Water presses harder, and harder with depth, and buried things are answered completely. So anything shorter than the Hold may take any shape, while a taller steep face needs a buttress everywhere more than a Hold below its top.

R2 — Only a push answers a push. Nothing can pull. Matter has no cohesion of its own and carries only pushes, plus the friction those pushes create. A buttress must stand on the side a thrust points toward, touching what it holds. The air's press gives small things a faint hold against crumbling, enough for a thick cup to keep its water, but that hold carries no load. So there are no ropes, beams, lintels, cantilevers, hinges, levers, nets, sails or bowstrings. Every span is an arch and every lift is a push from beneath. Anything that must hold a push from inside, such as a tank, pipe or barrel, can do so only by being pressed harder from outside, which in practice means being buried.

R3 — Thrust is passed, never lost. An answered thrust is not destroyed; it is handed on. Where two faces press on each other equally, as two people hip to hip or two houses sharing a wall do, the pushes cancel and nothing passes. A packed crowd, granary or town therefore needs holding only at its outside. Where the pushes are unequal (a tall thing against a short one, a leaning thing, the foot of an arch), the difference travels onward through unbroken contact and adds up link by link until it reaches the Ground. The last buttress of a row of five leaning houses carries the lean of all five plus its own. Remove any link and everything upstream of it is unanswered in the same instant. Long chains also bow sideways and fail unless something braces them along their length.

R4 — Weight grounds thrust. The Ground takes any thrust, but only if it arrives no flatter than the Ground's own repose allows. On earth, which reposes at one up for two across, the weight pressing down through a foot must be at least twice the sideways thrust that foot passes, or the foot skids. On bare bedrock, called a holdfast, equal weight is enough. Weight is what turns a sideways push downward, so loading a buttress from above strengthens it, and an unladen buttress slides however well it is placed. Every body lives with both sides of this. The heavier it is, the more thrust it can ground while it stays low, and (by R1) the harder it pushes when it stands tall.

R5 — Spreading is permanent; raising needs centering. Unanswered thrust spreads a thing until it is back at repose. A small excess does this slowly (creep, over minutes to years), and a large one does it all at once (a slump). Nothing slumped rises again by itself: raised matter can be built but never restored. Anything raised above the Hold must be built inside temporary support, called centering, that carries every thrust until the permanent buttresses are in place. The dangerous moment is always the striking of the centering. Living things are the one partial exception. They grow by laying new tissue against old, so they are their own centering, and they can slowly mend a small creep if they are braced in time. When they die, they slump like anything else.

3. How people live, work and organize society

Bodies. A grown person stands about twice the Hold (R1), so no adult stands upright alone for long; within minutes the legs begin to creep outward (R5). Children shorter than the Hold stand, run and climb freely. The Outgrowing, around the third year, is the day a child can no longer stand alone, and it is mourned as the first loss. From then until they stop growing, children are braced in frames through the day, or they set short and splayed. Adults on their own live low, sitting, squatting or crawling, and stand only where something supports them: a stall (a person-shaped niche with a hip-high front), a rail, or other people's hips. Anyone pressed from the hips down is held above them by the air, so hip-high walls line every room. Sleep, lying flat, needs nothing.

Hip-deep water presses the legs as the air presses the head, so the town pool is the one place an adult can stand without people or walls. It is where people stand as equals, and where assemblies, courtship and quarrels happen. Muscles push rather than pull. Heavy things ride on the head or back, and clothes are padded plates laid on like roof tiles, never hung, belted or tied (R2). People are a leaning kind: like forest trees, they grew tall because they were never alone.

Movement. Streets are hip-deep, hip-wide trenches. People walk them in files, pressed at the sides by the trench walls and front and back by one another. Only the head and heel of a file stoop below the Hold, and they are the heaviest walkers available, because they must ground the whole file's push (R3, R4). Goods travel on sledges and rollers in troughs, pushed from behind by low, heavy beasts, and the troughs keep long trains from bowing (R3). Water is the easy road. A hull is pressed inward by the water around it, so low-sided barges are simple and strong, and people and animals push them by wading behind.

Homes and towns. The natural house is a pointed dome sunk into the ground and heaped with earth. The heap answers the dome's outside and the dome's roundness answers its inside, so a village looks like a field of barrows with doors. Doors are rolled stones or leaning slabs, since nothing can hinge (R2). Walls taller than the Hold carry buttresses on both faces and curve between them, so each stretch arches sideways into its piers.

A town is one leaning body. Its houses share walls so their pushes cancel, and whatever does not cancel travels outward to the rim. The rim is a massive, low, stone-laden ring that exists to hold the town up, not to keep anyone out (R3, R4). Tall buildings can stand only in the middle, where they lean on everything around them, so every skyline rises and falls like a hill. The steeper the hill, the heavier the rim must be, and the rim's weight sets the height of the tallest tower (R1, R4). Windows need walls whose thrust is fully answered from outside. So light pours into the central towers and never into the rim, which carries everything and cannot be opened.

Work. The basic service is bearing someone else's push. Its unit is the lean, the push of one standing adult's hips, which is what one stall must answer, and rents are counted in leans borne. Weight is working capital. Stone set on a buttress raises how much thrust it can ground (R4), so a town's treasury literally sits on top of its rim piers, and withdrawing wealth weakens the town. Holdfasts are the scarcest land. Towns grow around them, and large towns reach distant holdfasts through long arcades that carry thrust across open country. The great trades are:
- Centerers, who build the temporary support for anything new (R5).
- Tappers, who trace thrust paths by ear, because a loaded chain rings when struck and a slack one thuds. The same fact gives music, played on stones wedged to pitch, and messages, tapped along the arcades.
- Wedgers, who walk the town at dawn re-driving the wedges the night's cold has loosened.
- Shorers, who line every hole as it is dug (R1).

Society and law. Physics sorts bodies. The heavy ground thrust best but push hardest when standing. The slight are cheap to hold up but can bear nothing (R1, R4). So in any gathering the slight stand at the center and the heavy stoop at the edge, and a crowd forms a human mound, tall in the middle and low at the rim. The smaller the group, the more of it must stoop, so households are large. A household is founded when its first arch is keyed and its centering struck before witnesses (R5). Elders, who have crept shorter over a lifetime, take the rim of their households, weighted with stone mantles.

Status is height. To stand is to be held, and the held see far, work at height and live in light. Power is weight. If the rim steps back, the central towers slump and the people in them drop to their knees, while the rim, already low, loses almost nothing. That strike, the Stoop, is the oldest political act.

Law is written as thrust paths. A deed lists what a house leans on and what leans on it, and a sale transfers both. Nothing that carries thrust may be removed without the consent of everything upstream and downstream of it (R3). The gravest crime is unanswering, which means withdrawing support without a replacement, and the law treats it as killing. Solitude is not a way of life but an injury. The dead no longer mend (R5), so they slump into mounds, and they are packed into the rim. Ancestors literally hold the living up.

4. What is easy, and what is hard

Easy:
- Staying put. Anything packed tight and held at its edge keeps its arrangement for centuries. Because equal pushes cancel (R3), density gets cheaper as it grows: a large crowd, store, forest or town needs less rim per member than a small one.
- Anything small. Below the Hold any shape stands (R1): tools, cups, bricks, children, small animals.
- Anything round, buried or under water. The ground itself holds wells, cellars, cisterns, tunnels and barrows, and water holds hulls and piers (R1, R2).
- Flattening and filling. Left alone, everything levels itself (R5). Roads and floors make themselves, and a hole that stops being shored fills in.
- Destruction. Remove the right link and everything upstream fails at once (R3). One stone can bring down a district, so demolition, sabotage and siege take little effort.
- Knowing where support is. Loaded chains ring, every steep slope betrays a buttress, and everyone feels it the moment someone stops holding them.
- Using weight. A load is never only a burden, because a load set on a buttress strengthens it (R4).
- Blocking. Pushed things jam across a narrow gap into a self-locking arch. A gate is a wedge, and a few heavy people can hold a passage.

Hard:
- Height. The push grows with the square of height (R1), and the excess must travel to a rim weighted to match (R3, R4). A tower twice as tall needs four times the holding and a wider town around it.
- Spanning. With no beams (R2), every gap needs an abutment on each side, an arch and centering (R5). Anything with only one support, such as an overhang, a ledge or a balcony, cannot be built at all.
- Pulling, lifting, hanging and tying (R2). Everything rises by ramp, wedge or push from beneath, and moves only by being pushed.
- Holding a push from inside (R2). There are no barrels, pipes, boilers or balloons bigger than a hand, and water cannot be raised or stored above ground.
- Solitude and new places (R1). A lone adult crawls, and an open plain is exhausting. A new settlement cannot let anyone stand until its rim is built, so its first builders work on their knees.
- Change and leaving (R3, R5). Nothing that carries thrust can be altered without first being re-centered, and no one who bears a load can simply walk away. Obligations are knotted along every thrust path, so old towns and old arrangements harden in place.
- Digging (R1). Every hole deeper than the Hold must be lined as it goes, so mines and deep footings are slow and deadly.
- Being light and strong at once (R4). The young and slight can bear nothing, and light structures skid.
- Undoing ruin (R5). A slump is final. Whatever falls must be rebuilt from the ground, under new centering.
- Sudden loosening. Anything that breaks contact even for a moment, such as a frost, a tremor, or a fire's swelling and cooling, unanswers everything above it at once (R3, R5).

temporality.code: irreversible relaxation, rate set by excess; instant cascades; staged ascent
temporality.note: one-way decay to repose (slow creep for small unanswered excess, instant slump for large); instantaneous failure of everything upstream when a link is lost; raising is staged, and striking the centering is the critical moment

conservation.code: load conserved: opposites cancel, net accumulates along chains to a sink
conservation.note: thrust is conserved: equal opposing pushes cancel, unequal ones pass their difference on and accumulate link by link until grounded; elevation is not conserved and, once lost, cannot be restored

agency.code: push-only; power = bearing or withdrawing support; growth self-scaffolds
agency.note: push-only actors whose power is to bear, reroute or withdraw thrust; withdrawal is the oldest political act (the Stoop) and the gravest crime (unanswering); organisms are their own centering through accretive growth

identity.code: relational: standing is a place in a support network, not a property
identity.note: relational: standing and shape exist only as answered thrust, so a thing is its place in a thrust network (what it leans on, what leans on it); a material is defined by its repose

scarcity.code: grounding capacity (ballast, anchor sites) scarce; height costs quadratically
scarcity.note: grounding capacity: ballast weight, holdfast bedrock and rim mass; height costs quadratically; adults must borrow standing, priced in leans borne

information_flow.code: load state legible via contact and shape; signals travel along support chains
information_flow.note: load state is legible through contact and shape: loaded chains ring, slack ones thud, every steep face betrays its buttress, withdrawal is felt at once; messages are tapped along load-bearing arcades

boundary_structure.code: interior cancels; outer boundary bears net load; small scale needs no support
boundary_structure.note: equal interior pushes cancel, so all net demand collects at the free outer boundary, a heavy, low, windowless rim, while light reaches only the held center; below a scale threshold (the Hold) nothing needs support

permitted_transformations.code: compression only; leveling free; raising needs scaffolding; collapse permanent
permitted_transformations.note: compression only (push, wedge, ramp, arch, burial); no pulling, tension, beams, cantilevers, hinges, or internal pressure held unburied above hand size; flattening is spontaneous, raising above the Hold requires centering, and a slump can be rebuilt but never restored

enforcement.code: automatic and instant physical enforcement; social law mirrors support chains
enforcement.note: automatic and impersonal: unanswered thrust spreads the thing at once and permanently; law mirrors the physics, requiring consent along the whole thrust path to remove a link and treating unanswering as killing

worlds.title: The Unbroken Watch: Where Only the Watched Stay Themselves
worlds.text:
The Unbroken Watch: Where Only the Watched Stay Themselves

1. The core principle

Physics in this world has two halves. Process works much as ours does: things fall, burn, flow, grow and react. Persistence works differently, because nothing holds on to its own particulars. The quantity at stake is thisness. It means the lasting particulars (marks, grain, shape, wording, memory) that make this stone this stone rather than just a stone. Position, posture and motion are not thisness. Left alone, thisness drains away, and every particular thing slides toward the most ordinary member of its kind.

Only one force runs against the drain, and that is vigil: a waking mind's attention, kept on a thing without a break. Vigil cannot create anything, and it cannot restore anything. It can only keep. So the detail of the world is a record of the attention it has received. Where minds have watched long and closely, the world is dense with particulars. Where no mind has watched, it is typical. The near face of the moon is watched every night by every eye on the planet, and it still carries every mark it has taken since the first eyes looked up. Its far side is smooth grey.

Animals keep too. Herds post sentinels. Birds and dolphins sleep with one half of the brain at a time, so they keep themselves around the clock, which makes them the most individual creatures in the wild. Faces, texts, cities and species are all built up from vigil. Only the plainest stuff of the world lasts without vigil, present or past, and minds are the only keepers.

2. The laws

R1. The Keeping. Only vigil holds thisness. Vigil is attention from a waking mind, aimed at a thing, without a break.
- Vigil resists every loss of thisness, whatever the cause: lapse, wear, rot, fire, blade, healing, dying.
- It holds harder the more thisness is at stake. Planing a rough plank meets almost no resistance. Breaking an old carved door while someone watches it meets a great deal.
- It does not resist motion. It also does not resist any change that adds more particulars than it takes away. So under watch, detail tends only to build up.
- A gap shorter than the grace (about one slow breath, five seconds) does not count, so blinks and glances are safe. A doze, a distraction or a walk to the door breaks the vigil.
- A vigil passes from one keeper to the next only if the new keeper takes hold within the grace. In practice, keepers overlap.

R2. The Lapse. Whatever is not kept loses thisness.
- It goes typical first. Then it steps down a ladder of kinds toward its materials. It stops only at the Ground: stone, water, air and grey. Grey is the fine silt that all made and once-living things end as.
- An unkept book goes from this book, to a typical book of its sort, to cliché, to words without sense, to marks, to blank paper, to pulp, to grey.
- Lapse runs one way only. A renewed vigil stops it where it is and restores nothing.
- It runs fastest on what is intricate and new. Detail that formed an hour ago fades within hours if no one sees it. A thing that is already typical has almost nothing left to lose.
- Why the Ground needs no keeping at all is the oldest open question in this world's physics.

R3. The Grain. A vigil keeps a thing only down to the finest detail its keeper can make out.
- Sight keeps surfaces at a distance, but only in light. Touch keeps shape and texture within reach. Hearing and smell keep only the fact that the thing is still there and still its kind.
- Grain gets coarser with distance and with breadth. Someone watching a whole square keeps its buildings but not their carvings.
- Grain gets deeper with understanding. A keeper who knows a clock's gears keeps the gears; one who sees only a box keeps a box. A reader makes out letters where someone who cannot read sees only texture.
- When several people watch one thing, everything any of them can make out is kept.

R4. Tenure. An unbroken vigil cures what it keeps, and that stored keeping is called tenure.
- Tenure grows with the square of the unbroken span, so a vigil twice as long cures four times as deep. A break keeps the tenure already gained, but the count starts again from zero.
- Tenure is spent as a shield. An unwatched thing draws it down and lapses slowly until it runs out, then at full speed.
- Forty unbroken days of watching let a newborn sleep a night alone with almost no loss. Forty separate days of daytime watching give it less than a hundredth as much.
- Kinds have tenure too: the sum of every vigil ever kept over any of their members. Ancient kinds such as human, oak, bread and wheel are nearly unshakable. A new kind, such as the first machine of its design, slides into the nearest older kind it resembles. A kind whose members no one keeps drains away over generations.

R5. The Burden. Lapse is never cancelled, only moved.
- Whatever thisness a vigil saves, the keeper carries as weariness. It is light for a long-cured wall, heavy for a newborn and crushing for a burning house.
- Everyone keeping the same detail shares the load. But each keeper can carry only so much, and any excess drains the keeper's own thisness instead.
- Weariness is shed only in sleep, where it burns off as dreams. That is why dreams are full of faces and places going typical.
- A sleeper keeps nothing, not even themself. A burdened sleeper whom no one keeps discharges part of the day's weight into their own thisness. A keeper who refuses to sleep starts to lapse while awake.

These laws are measured, not believed. The grace is timed with water clocks. Tenure is calibrated by leaving fresh-cut tiles unwatched for set hours and comparing them with twins that were kept.

3. How people live

Night and household. Sight needs light (R3), so night is the daily tide of lapse, and lamp oil is the second staple after grain.
- Every household runs a Round, a rota of night watches with overlapping handovers. The incoming keeper says "I have it," and the outgoing keeper does not look away until they hear it (R1).
- Two adults can keep each other by taking turns. A household with a baby needs three.
- Beds face a keeper's chair.
- On the dark of the moon, called the Grey Night, whole streets keep watch together with every lamp lit.
- Blind people keep by touch and hearing, so darkness costs them nothing. They are prized as night-keepers and hold a sleeper's face with their fingertips.

Birth and childhood. In the womb a child is kept only by the mother's coarse sense of her own body (R3). So every newborn arrives with the same typical face, and its particulars build up only under watch (R1).
- The Forty Days is an unbroken vigil over the cradle, kept by relays of relatives. Its burden eases as the child cures (R4, R5), and it ends in a naming feast.
- A newborn left unwatched in its first weeks becomes a changeling. It is healthy but has gone typical, with none of the particulars its parents had come to know (R2).
- A mother who only listens in the dark keeps her child from dying, but not from going typical.
- Because tenure compounds, a childhood kept without a break lasts a lifetime. An adult who was neglected as a child goes typical after a few lonely weeks.

Keeping one another. A well-kept adult carries years of tenure, so one unkept night costs little: a minor memory turns generic, a small scar fades, a quirk of handwriting smooths out.
- After a month of unkept nights, friends find the face hard to picture. After a year with no one who knows them, a person has gone typical.
- Strangers' eyes keep a face, but only someone who understands a person keeps their self (R3). So everyone has a night-keeper who knows them, usually a spouse, sibling or old friend.
- What is shared is kept, and what no one else knows fades night by night. Secrets last only if they are told to one's keeper.
- No one can keep their own face without a mirror.
- The marriage vow is "I will keep you."
- People who have gone typical, such as hermits, lone sailors and prisoners held in solitary, are called Typicals. They are interchangeable and hard to identify. They are pitied, and sometimes hired for exactly that reason.

Work. The unit of account is the keep: one hour of one keeper's vigil.
- Professional keeping is ranked by grain. Far-keepers in towers hold skylines and walls cheaply. Near-keepers hold faces, texts and goods. Deep-keepers understand what they watch, as machinists, physicians and scholars do, and they are the elite.
- Unsleeping orders keep a city's oldest treasures, such as a charter stone or a founding library, in relays unbroken for centuries. These are the most tenured and hardest-to-destroy objects in the world (R1, R4).
- Every workshop has a curing room where new work sits under lamp and keeper until it sets.
- The fire-watch is night watch and fire brigade in one. Ranks of keepers stare a fire down in rotating files, sharing its burden and holding it in check while others put it out (R5). Recruits who hold on past their limit come away grey-struck, with their own faces and memories drained.
- Making things goes easily under watch. Breaking old, particular things does not (R1), so demolition workers wear hoods.
- Mastery, the saying goes, is work that does not mind being watched.

Medicine and death. Bandages are blinds. A closely watched wound will not rot, but it will not heal either (R1).
- Every treatment is a choice between holding and letting go. A scar is a wound that was looked at too often while it healed.
- Most natural deaths come in unkept sleep (R5).
- Families hold the dying in relays for as long as they can bear the burden. When everyone is ready, they perform the Turning. The watchers turn their backs at once, and the dying person closes their eyes and stops holding on. Death comes in the first moment when no one, the dying included, is keeping. If one child peeks, the dying person lingers.
- Wealthy houses keep dying elders as the Held: suspended for months or years, neither recovering nor dying.
- After death, the wake keeps the body's face for the mourners. Then the body is let go to grey.
- A portrait of the dead lasts as long as someone who loved them keeps looking at it. When the last of those people dies, the portrait slides into a stranger's face. This is called the second death.

Cities, property and law. Streets are laid out so everything can be seen: every facade faces a window, and lamps burn at every corner.
- A hidden room goes typical ("what you hide, you lose"), so treasuries are glass halls with keepers.
- A family back from a long journey finds a house that could be anyone's.
- The cost of owning a thing is the cost of keeping it. Old and typical things are cheap; new and particular things are expensive.
- Money is coin, never paper. A stamped disc is already typical, and a signed note fades (R2).
- The poor live among typical cups, clothes and houses, which last and belong to nobody in particular. The rich live among particulars and count their wealth in keepers.
- Tearing down anything a community watches requires averting: its watchers must agree to look away (R1).
- A protest is a vigil. A relay of protesters can hold a building against demolition, paying with their own weariness.
- The harshest punishments are solitary darkness and exile into the unwatched country. Both are understood as unmaking.

Knowledge and travel. Books are kept by readers, and only by readers of their script (R3).
- A new book is set by a reading vigil: it is read aloud in unbroken relay for days (R4).
- Books in a dead script drain toward marks.
- Letters, contracts and laws are written in stock formulas. A formula is already typical and survives; a particular sentence fades (R2).
- Couriers read their letters as they ride.
- Coded messages barely survive a day unread, because a random string is all particulars and has no kind to fall back on.
- Travelers go in threes.
- The unwatched country, called the Plain, has weather but no landmarks. The backs of mountains are smooth. The only fixed points are ruins, places someone once kept.
- A new settlement takes generations to become a place.
- Northern peoples build during the white nights of midsummer, when new work can cure in unbroken light.

4. What is easy, what is hard

Easy:
- Preserving the old and the typical. An ancient wall, a standard brick or a mass-made cup needs almost no keeping and lasts indefinitely (R2, R4).
- Healing small wounds without scars: cover them and don't look (R1).
- Holding a moment. A dying parent can be held through days of goodbyes (R1, R5).
- Sensing decay. A trained keeper feels rot, cracks, fever or fire as weariness before anyone can see it (R5).
- Enriching whatever is watched. Busy, watched places grow dense with history, and making things goes smoothly under watch (R1).
- Public safety. People and buildings watched by many are hard to damage, so harm needs darkness (R1, R5).
- Shared memory. Whatever a community looks at together, it keeps (R1, R3).
- Disappearing. A year with no one who knows you makes you no one in particular (R2).

Hard:
- Anything new. Every invention, breed, book and person must be watched without a break until cured, and new kinds slide back into old ones. The physics itself pulls toward tradition (R4).
- Privacy and solitude. Unshared memories, hidden rooms and unread diaries fade, and going unknown erases you (R2, R3).
- Letting go. Healing means looking away, the dying need the Turning, and grief lasts as long as you cannot stop attending to it (R1).
- Changing what is established. Demolition and reform need collective averting, and one stubborn watcher can stall them (R1).
- Rest. Nobody simply sleeps. You need a keeper, and the more you kept today, the heavier you are to keep tonight (R5).
- Darkness. Every unlit hour is lapse for whatever no one is touching, and moonless nights are dangerous (R3).
- Distance. Letters decay into cliché, secrets cannot travel, lone journeys erase the traveler, and the Plain cannot be mapped (R2, R3).
- Knowledge outliving its knowers. When a script or a craft loses the last keeper who understands it, its books and machines drain toward marks and scrap (R3, R4).
- Fast destruction. Fire and violence outrun any keeper's limit, and resisting them costs the keepers themselves (R5).
- Scale. A society can hold only as much particularity as it has waking hours. Every precious thing competes for keepers, and no machine can be more intricate than its keepers understand (R3, R5).
worlds.principle: Physics in this world has two halves. Process works much as ours does: things fall, burn, flow, grow and react. Persistence works differently, because nothing holds on to its own particulars. The quantity at stake is thisness. It means the lasting particulars (marks, grain, shape, wording, memory) that make this stone this stone rather than just a stone. Position, posture and motion are not thisness. Left alone, thisness drains away, and every particular thing slides toward the most ordinary member of its kind. Only one force runs against the drain, and that is vigil: a waking mind's attention, kept on a thing without a break. Vigil cannot create anything, and it cannot restore anything. It can only keep. So the detail of the world is a record of the attention it has received. Where minds have watched long and closely, the world is dense with particulars. Where no mind has watched, it is typical. The near face of the moon is watched every night by every eye on the planet, and it still carries every mark it has taken since the first eyes looked up. Its far side is smooth grey. Animals keep too. Herds post sentinels. Birds and dolphins sleep with one half of the brain at a time, so they keep themselves around the clock, which makes them the most individual creatures in the wild. Faces, texts, cities and species are all built up from vigil. Only the plainest stuff of the world lasts without vigil, present or past, and minds are the only keepers. 2. The laws

rules.statement: The Keeping. Only vigil holds thisness. Vigil is attention from a waking mind, aimed at a thing, without a break. - Vigil resists every loss of thisness, whatever the cause: lapse, wear, rot, fire, blade, healing, dying. - It holds harder the more thisness is at stake. Planing a rough plank meets almost no resistance. Breaking an old carved door while someone watches it meets a great deal. - It does not resist motion. It also does not resist any change that adds more particulars than it takes away. So under watch, detail tends only to build up. - A gap shorter than the grace (about one slow breath, five seconds) does not count, so blinks and glances are safe. A doze, a distraction or a walk to the door breaks the vigil. - A vigil passes from one keeper to the next only if the new keeper takes hold within the grace. In practice, keepers overlap.

The Lapse. Whatever is not kept loses thisness. - It goes typical first. Then it steps down a ladder of kinds toward its materials. It stops only at the Ground: stone, water, air and grey. Grey is the fine silt that all made and once-living things end as. - An unkept book goes from this book, to a typical book of its sort, to cliché, to words without sense, to marks, to blank paper, to pulp, to grey. - Lapse runs one way only. A renewed vigil stops it where it is and restores nothing. - It runs fastest on what is intricate and new. Detail that formed an hour ago fades within hours if no one sees it. A thing that is already typical has almost nothing left to lose. - Why the Ground needs no keeping at all is the oldest open question in this world's physics.

The Grain. A vigil keeps a thing only down to the finest detail its keeper can make out. - Sight keeps surfaces at a distance, but only in light. Touch keeps shape and texture within reach. Hearing and smell keep only the fact that the thing is still there and still its kind. - Grain gets coarser with distance and with breadth. Someone watching a whole square keeps its buildings but not their carvings. - Grain gets deeper with understanding. A keeper who knows a clock's gears keeps the gears; one who sees only a box keeps a box. A reader makes out letters where someone who cannot read sees only texture. - When several people watch one thing, everything any of them can make out is kept.

Tenure. An unbroken vigil cures what it keeps, and that stored keeping is called tenure. - Tenure grows with the square of the unbroken span, so a vigil twice as long cures four times as deep. A break keeps the tenure already gained, but the count starts again from zero. - Tenure is spent as a shield. An unwatched thing draws it down and lapses slowly until it runs out, then at full speed. - Forty unbroken days of watching let a newborn sleep a night alone with almost no loss. Forty separate days of daytime watching give it less than a hundredth as much. - Kinds have tenure too: the sum of every vigil ever kept over any of their members. Ancient kinds such as human, oak, bread and wheel are nearly unshakable. A new kind, such as the first machine of its design, slides into the nearest older kind it resembles. A kind whose members no one keeps drains away over generations.

The Burden. Lapse is never cancelled, only moved. - Whatever thisness a vigil saves, the keeper carries as weariness. It is light for a long-cured wall, heavy for a newborn and crushing for a burning house. - Everyone keeping the same detail shares the load. But each keeper can carry only so much, and any excess drains the keeper's own thisness instead. - Weariness is shed only in sleep, where it burns off as dreams. That is why dreams are full of faces and places going typical. - A sleeper keeps nothing, not even themself. A burdened sleeper whom no one keeps discharges part of the day's weight into their own thisness. A keeper who refuses to sleep starts to lapse while awake.

temporality.code: one-way lapse, fastest on the new; tenure ~ span squared; relays within grace
temporality.note: Lapse is irreversible and stepwise down a ladder of kinds to the Ground; renewed vigil halts it but restores nothing. Rate rises with intricacy and newness, near zero for the typical. Unbroken vigil stores tenure growing with the square of the span; a break keeps tenure but restarts the count; unwatched things spend tenure, lapsing slowly, then at full speed. Failure is buffered and gradual, not an instant cascade. Gaps under the 5 s grace do not count, so handovers overlap. Night and compulsory sleep impose a daily tide of lapse. New work must cure under vigil.

conservation.code: lapse never cancelled, only moved into keepers as burden, shed only in sleep
conservation.note: Whatever thisness a vigil saves, the keeper carries as weariness: light for a cured wall, crushing for a burning house. Co-keepers of the same detail share it in parallel; each has a capacity, and overflow drains the keeper's own thisness. Sleep is the only sink (weariness burns off as dreams), but sleepers keep nothing: left unkept, a burdened sleeper discharges part of the load into themself; kept, they weigh more on the night-keeper. Nothing is signed, so nothing cancels; burden moves along keeping chains through time, leaking away at each sleep.

agency.code: keep-only: vigil holds, never creates or restores; power = keeping or averting
agency.note: Only waking minds keep, animals included; objects and the Ground are passive. Making and accretion go easily under watch, while destroying particulars is resisted in proportion to what is at stake, so power over established things lies in withholding attention (averting, the Turning, hooded demolition) or massing it (fire-watch, protest vigils). Self-keeping is partial: a waking mind keeps what it can perceive of itself, never its own face without a mirror, and nothing of itself asleep. Growth does not self-scaffold; new work must be cured under vigil.

identity.code: relational-epistemic: particulars last only while known; the unknown go typical
identity.note: A held property, not a network position: thisness (marks, grain, memory) lasts only through keepers who can make it out, and only a keeper who understands a person keeps their self rather than their face. Identity is a stock sustained by being known: neglected people become interchangeable Typicals, unwatched newborns become changelings, portraits suffer a second death when the last loving watcher dies, and new kinds merge into the nearest old kind. Kinds hold their identity through tenure summed over all members.

scarcity.code: particularity capped by keeper-hours, burden capacity, light and understanding
scarcity.note: The keep (one keeper-hour) is the unit of account. Each keeper carries only so much burden per waking day, sleep is compulsory and sleepers must be kept, so rotas absorb a large share of waking hours (two adults to keep a couple, three with a baby). Sight needs light, making lamp oil the second staple. Grain rises with understanding, so deep-keepers are an elite and no machine can be more intricate than its keepers understand. Old and typical things are cheap; new and particular things are dear.

information_flow.code: information lasts only while perceived; unshared detail fades toward formula
information_flow.note: A record lasts only while some keeper can make it out: books need readers of their script, secrets must be told to one's keeper, letters decay into cliche in transit unless the courier reads them, and coded messages barely survive a day unread because a random string has no kind to fall back on. Stock formulas survive because they are already typical. Burden doubles as a sense: keepers feel rot, cracks, fever and fire as weariness before they show. What a community watches together, it remembers.

boundary_structure.code: Ground needs no keeping, typical almost none; kept zone ends at keepers' grain
boundary_structure.note: The floor is the Ground (stone, water, air, grey), which needs no keeping; typical things sit near it and lose little. Above it, what is kept is exactly what some keeper can make out: surfaces in light at a distance, shape within reach by touch, inner workings only through understanding, coarsening with distance and breadth, pooled across keepers. Hidden interiors, far sides and the unwatched Plain lapse. The temporal edge is the 5 s grace. No interior cancellation: exposure, not enclosure, protects.

permitted_transformations.code: watch resists only net loss; lapse one-way down kinds; nothing restores
permitted_transformations.note: A kept thing may move and may gain particulars; any change that removes more than it adds is resisted in proportion to the thisness at stake (planing a rough plank is easy, breaking a watched carved door is hard). Unkept things step down the ladder of kinds toward the Ground, and renewed vigil halts but never reverses this. New kinds slide into the nearest older kind unless cured. Healing and dying require looking away; destroying watched things requires averting.

enforcement.code: automatic physical lapse, buffered by tenure; social law mirrors keeping duties
enforcement.note: The laws enforce themselves: lapse and burden follow automatically and are measured, not believed (water-clock grace, tile tenure calibration). Resistance under watch is immediate, but lapse is delayed and gradual wherever tenure has built up, so neglect is punished late rather than by instant cascade. Social institutions mirror the physics: household Rounds, the vow 'I will keep you', averting before demolition, protest as vigil, and punishment by solitary darkness or exile into the Plain, understood as unmaking.

worlds.title: The Turning Deep: Where To Be Is To Turn
worlds.text:
The Turning Deep: Where To Be Is To Turn

1. THE CORE PRINCIPLE

The world has one substance, the Deep. It has no grain, no parts and no weight of its own. All it can do is flow. Everything else is a whirlpool in the Deep.

Nothing is made of anything. The Deep passes through every whirl all the time: it is drawn in at the rim and let go through the eye. So no thing keeps its material for even an instant. Only the turning lasts, and a thing is simply its turning. Four properties describe any thing completely:
- hand: deasil (clockwise seen from above) or widdershins (counterclockwise).
- turn: how strongly it rotates. This does the work that mass and charge do in other worlds.
- eye: a tight eye makes a hard, dense thing. A wide eye makes a soft, diffuse one.
- draw: how hard it drinks the Deep. This is its weight.

Some examples:
- A stone is a fine checkerboard of tight whirls of both hands. It is still inside and quiet from outside.
- Spume is made of loose, wide-eyed whirls that last only moments.
- A person is a braid of thousands of small whirls turning in step around one heart-eye. Each person has a net hand.

Whirls act on each other in only one way. Each one stirs the whole Deep around it, instantly and to any distance, and the stir fades as distance grows. There is no pushing, no contact force and no light. Every motion, every sense and every exchange is one whirl being carried or fed by the stir of others.

The world is itself a whirl, the largest one known, called the Maelstrom:
- It turns deasil around a calm central Eye, with a Throat beneath the Eye.
- Fresh Deep pours in across the far Rim. Spent Deep leaves down the Throat and is never felt again.
- People live on the Floor, a broad shelf of settled whirls that slopes gently toward the Eye.

The world, like everything in it, is a standing shape with no permanent substance.

2. THE LAWS

R1. The Draw.
- Every whirl drinks the Deep. This pulls the Deep, and everything in it, into an inward spiral toward the whirl's eye.
- The pull grows with the draw. Between two people it is too faint to notice, except as the dust that circles a sleeper.
- Nothing falls straight. A drawn thing circles whatever draws it, and each circuit is tighter and faster than the last. At half the distance it moves twice as fast.
- So no orbit is stable, and everything ends at an eye.
- At the scale of a hand, the Draw is weight. A dropped cup spirals down and lands a little deasil of the spot below where it was let go.
- At the scale of the world, the Draw is drift. The Deep near the Floor turns slower than the Deep above it, so the Floor layer is drawn inward harder. The whole Floor creeps toward the Eye, and the heaviest things creep fastest.
- A round is one full circuit of the Eye. At half the distance from the Eye, a round lasts a quarter as long.
- "Down," "inward" and "older" are the same word.

R2. The Twin Law.
- Turn is never created or destroyed, only divided.
- A whirl can only be spun up together with an equal twin of the opposite hand.
- When equal opposites meet, both vanish into froth: a fine spray of tiny twin pairs. Froth is what heat is.
- A little froth feeds whatever it touches, and too much tears it. Left alone, froth frays into still Deep, which is cold.
- A whirl that takes in a smaller whirl of its own hand merges with it. That is eating and growth.
- A whirl that takes in the opposite hand has part of itself cancelled. That is burning.

R3. The Law of Company.
- No whirl, and no braid of whirls, can move its own heart by moving its parts. Things move only in each other's stir.
- Two whirls of the same hand circle their shared center. If their eyes come within three eye-widths of each other, they merge into one larger whirl, and neither survives as itself.
- Two whirls of opposite hand and equal turn travel together in a straight line, side by side. The widdershins one is on the left of the direction of travel and the deasil one on the right.
- The closer such a pair is, the faster it goes. If their eyes touch, both cancel (R2).
- A pair of opposite hands but unequal turn travels in a circle that bends toward the stronger partner.

R4. The Law of Shear.
- A whirl lives by feeding on shear: faster Deep rubbing past slower Deep.
- With too little shear, a whirl starves and unravels. Its turn does not vanish (R2). It widens into a faint, slow swirl that spreads through its surroundings.
- With more shear than its turn can hold, a whirl is torn to froth.
- Tight whirls need little shear and can withstand a lot. Loose ones need steady, gentle shear.
- Around the Maelstrom, shear quadruples each time the distance to the Eye halves. So every kind of thing has a band where it can last:
  - The Rim starves things.
  - The Wall around the Eye tears them.
  - Inside the Eye the Deep turns as one rigid piece with no shear at all. It is perfectly calm, and everything in it slowly unravels.
- Still Deep anywhere is the same death. A sealed room is a small Eye.

R5. The Mirror.
- Every solid boundary answers each nearby whirl with a mirror-whirl of the opposite hand. The mirror stands as far behind the wall as the whirl stands in front of it.
- The mirror is not a thing. Nothing can touch it or feed on it, but it stirs like a real whirl.
- So by R3, a lone whirl beside a wall is paired with its own reflection and slides along the wall. A deasil whirl keeps the wall on its left, and a widdershins whirl keeps it on its right.
- It slides as fast as it would travel with a real partner at twice its distance from the wall.
- In a round walled room, a lone whirl circles the center, faster near the wall. Only at the exact center do the mirrors balance and let it rest.
- A pair that meets a wall head-on splits. The widdershins partner slides off to the left and the deasil partner to the right.
- The more a wall blocks the Deep, the stronger its mirror, and the more it starves the room behind it (R4).

3. HOW PEOPLE LIVE

Pairs and Hands
- Every birth is a twin birth (R2). Each child is spun from its parents' shear together with an equal twin of the other hand.
- The pair, not the person, is the basic unit of society.
- Twins get mirrored names, such as Neva and Aven, and are raised a stride apart.
- Twins share "the even bowl": identical portions all their lives. Twins who drift apart in turn can only walk in circles.
- Society is made of two equal Hands, Deasil and Widdershins.
- Every harvest comes up half of each hand (R2). Each Hand eats only its own half, because the other half would burn it.
- A person whose twin has died is called a half.

Moving
- A matched pair with hearts a stride apart travels at a walking pace. At a hand's breadth apart it goes seven times faster.
- Closer still is the courier's gamble. Hearts touching is the embrace that burns.
- Turning a corner costs a trim pellet: a crumb of your own hand, swallowed by the partner on the side you want to turn toward. The other partner must later swallow a matching pellet, so long routes leave couriers swollen with turn.
- Over long distances the Maelstrom's shear bends every straight course, so long routes are drawn as spirals.
- Journeys end at walls, where the partners split apart (R5).
- Alone, a person crosses open ground only as far as the Floor's drift carries her. Otherwise she rides wall-roads, which carry Deasil traffic one way and Widdershins traffic the other.
- A loner can go only one way along any wall, and a gap in the wall stops her dead.

Company and touch
- Two people of the same Hand who stop to talk slowly circle each other. Two people of opposite Hands who stop to talk begin to walk.
- People of the same Hand keep their hearts three heart-widths apart.
- A crush of one Hand merges at its center into one enormous whirl. This is the worst disaster a town can suffer.
- Mixed crowds shed pairs from their edges and scatter.
- The only gathering that stays still is a walled checkerboard. The Hands alternate in square cells, and the walls stand on the outer cell edges so the mirrors complete the pattern.
- Councils, courts and theaters are built this way. One empty or wrongly filled seat sets the whole room creeping.
- Every round room has one still seat at its center, and whoever sits in it presides.

Towns
- A town is built as a pair: a Deasil half and a Widdershins half on either side of a long central avenue.
- Like any pair, the town travels, very slowly, along its avenue. Its heading bends toward whichever half holds more turn (R3).
- So the balance of people, food and stored counterstock between the halves steers the town. Importing one Hand's goods turns the town toward that half.
- The steady business of civic life is holding the town's band: keeping the avenue aimed at the Rim against the Floor's inward creep.
- A balanced town climbs outward. An unbalanced town circles and loses ground.
- Each Hand lives in its own half, so every family straddles the avenue. Twins sleep on opposite sides and meet in the middle.
- Towns are founded near the Rim, grow rich as they sink into stronger shear, and are torn apart near the Wall. An old town is an inward town.

Keeping
- Nothing keeps without shear (R4), so walls are screens and lattices.
- Every building trades mirror against feed. Solid walls make fast wall-roads but starve the rooms behind them. Open screens feed the rooms but barely carry anyone.
- Food keeps only in larders with the Deep flowing through them.
- Records are knotted whirl-patterns that unravel when their flow stops. So archives are carousels, and reciters keep the oldest texts turning by rote.
- No one sleeps in a closed room.

Work
- Tenders keep the Deep moving through larders, archives, houses and workshops. It is the largest trade.
- Spinners make everything in twin lots: every pot, blade and bolt of cloth is made once in each hand. The unwanted twin is called counterstock and is stored far from its partner.
- Burners make warmth by bringing measured amounts of counterstock together into froth. They work in burn-houses set apart from everything else.
- Stirrers refine materials by stirring. In any stirred basin, the heavy things creep to the eye and the loose things linger at the rim.
- Matchers weigh turn and pair strangers of equal strength for journeys.
- Couriers are matched pairs. It is the fastest trade and the deadliest.
- Ledgerers keep the turn-ledger. Turn is conserved, so every gain has its counterpart somewhere, and the ledger records where every twin lies. Unexplained turn is evidence of a crime.
- Listeners read the stir:
  - A lone whirl's stir carries far.
  - A pair's two stirs cancel at a distance, and the closer the pair, the quieter.
  - So loners are loud and pairs are quiet.
  - The combined stir of every loner is the Hum. It is faint at the Rim and deafening near the Wall.

Time, death and belief
- Places are given as a band and a phase (position around the circuit).
- Every band keeps its own calendar, because a round gets shorter further inward. Inner lives run hot and short; Rim lives run slow and thin.
- Death is unraveling. The dead widen into faint swirls that linger in still places, so a graveyard can be felt as a faint net turn of one Hand. The dead do not vanish; they widen.
- The gravest crime is a forced merge: holding a person of your own Hand within three heart-widths until they merge. It kills the victim, enlarges the killer, and shows in the ledger as sudden unexplained turn.
- Stillness is the great taboo. The common blessing is "keep turning."
- Two stories frame the world:
  - The Heap: every heavy thing ever made, carried in by the creep, lies unraveling in the calm beneath the Eye.
  - The Counter-World: by R2 the Maelstrom must have a widdershins twin. By R3 that twin would be traveling with it, in a straight line, toward something no one has felt.

4. WHAT IS EASY, WHAT IS HARD

Easy:
- Anything circular: wheels, mills, orbits, circulation. Turning is the default state of everything.
- Straight travel for a matched pair. Once moving, a balanced pair needs nothing to keep going.
- Separating things. Stir a basin and wait. A long wall sorts a crowd by Hand, sending Deasil one way and Widdershins the other.
- Joining like to like. Welding, alloying, growing and eating only need whirls of the same hand brought within three eye-widths.
- Heat exactly when it is wanted, from measured counterstock.
- Knowing instantly where every loud thing in the world is.
- Exact accounts, because turn always balances.

Hard:
- Keeping anything: storage, archives, monuments, preserved food. A closed container kills whatever is inside it.
- Going outward, or even staying put. The Draw wins in the end.
- Being alone. A single person cannot cross open ground, turn back along a wall, or get past a gap in it.
- Making just one of anything, and getting rid of its twin.
- Touch: embracing, crowding, or packing people or goods of either Hand close together.
- Turning, stopping and aiming:
  - A released stone just spirals down.
  - Only a twinshot, a matched pair of pellets, flies straight, and it bends toward its stronger half.
  - Every corner costs a pellet.
- Hiding a loner, and finding a close pair.
- Being felt far away. Pairs are quiet, so a distant signal needs a strong lone whirl whose twin is kept far off.

worlds.principle: The world has one substance, the Deep. It has no grain, no parts and no weight of its own. All it can do is flow. Everything else is a whirlpool in the Deep. Nothing is made of anything. The Deep passes through every whirl all the time: it is drawn in at the rim and let go through the eye. So no thing keeps its material for even an instant. Only the turning lasts, and a thing is simply its turning. Four properties describe any thing completely: - hand: deasil (clockwise seen from above) or widdershins (counterclockwise). - turn: how strongly it rotates. This does the work that mass and charge do in other worlds. - eye: a tight eye makes a hard, dense thing. A wide eye makes a soft, diffuse one. - draw: how hard it drinks the Deep. This is its weight. Some examples: - A stone is a fine checkerboard of tight whirls of both hands. It is still inside and quiet from outside. - Spume is made of loose, wide-eyed whirls that last only moments. - A person is a braid of thousands of small whirls turning in step around one heart-eye. Each person has a net hand. Whirls act on each other in only one way. Each one stirs the whole Deep around it, instantly and to any distance, and the stir fades as distance grows. There is no pushing, no contact force and no light. Every motion, every sense and every exchange is one whirl being carried or fed by the stir of others. The world is itself a whirl, the largest one known, called the Maelstrom: - It turns deasil around a calm central Eye, with a Throat beneath the Eye. - Fresh Deep pours in across the far Rim. Spent Deep leaves down the Throat and is never felt again. - People live on the Floor, a broad shelf of settled whirls that slopes gently toward the Eye. The world, like everything in it, is a standing shape with no permanent substance. 2. THE LAWS

rules.statement: The Draw. - Every whirl drinks the Deep. This pulls the Deep, and everything in it, into an inward spiral toward the whirl's eye. - The pull grows with the draw. Between two people it is too faint to notice, except as the dust that circles a sleeper. - Nothing falls straight. A drawn thing circles whatever draws it, and each circuit is tighter and faster than the last. At half the distance it moves twice as fast. - So no orbit is stable, and everything ends at an eye. - At the scale of a hand, the Draw is weight. A dropped cup spirals down and lands a little deasil of the spot below where it was let go. - At the scale of the world, the Draw is drift. The Deep near the Floor turns slower than the Deep above it, so the Floor layer is drawn inward harder. The whole Floor creeps toward the Eye, and the heaviest things creep fastest. - A round is one full circuit of the Eye. At half the distance from the Eye, a round lasts a quarter as long. - "Down," "inward" and "older" are the same word.

The Twin Law. - Turn is never created or destroyed, only divided. - A whirl can only be spun up together with an equal twin of the opposite hand. - When equal opposites meet, both vanish into froth: a fine spray of tiny twin pairs. Froth is what heat is. - A little froth feeds whatever it touches, and too much tears it. Left alone, froth frays into still Deep, which is cold. - A whirl that takes in a smaller whirl of its own hand merges with it. That is eating and growth. - A whirl that takes in the opposite hand has part of itself cancelled. That is burning.

The Law of Company. - No whirl, and no braid of whirls, can move its own heart by moving its parts. Things move only in each other's stir. - Two whirls of the same hand circle their shared center. If their eyes come within three eye-widths of each other, they merge into one larger whirl, and neither survives as itself. - Two whirls of opposite hand and equal turn travel together in a straight line, side by side. The widdershins one is on the left of the direction of travel and the deasil one on the right. - The closer such a pair is, the faster it goes. If their eyes touch, both cancel (R2). - A pair of opposite hands but unequal turn travels in a circle that bends toward the stronger partner.

The Law of Shear. - A whirl lives by feeding on shear: faster Deep rubbing past slower Deep. - With too little shear, a whirl starves and unravels. Its turn does not vanish (R2). It widens into a faint, slow swirl that spreads through its surroundings. - With more shear than its turn can hold, a whirl is torn to froth. - Tight whirls need little shear and can withstand a lot. Loose ones need steady, gentle shear. - Around the Maelstrom, shear quadruples each time the distance to the Eye halves. So every kind of thing has a band where it can last: - The Rim starves things. - The Wall around the Eye tears them. - Inside the Eye the Deep turns as one rigid piece with no shear at all. The mirror stands as far behind the wall as the whirl stands in front of it. - The mirror is not a thing. Only at the exact center do the mirrors balance and let it rest. - A pair that meets a wall head-on splits. The widdershins partner slides off to the left and the deasil partner to the right. - The more a wall blocks the Deep, the stronger its mirror, and the more it starves the room behind it (R4).

Knowing instantly where every loud thing in the world is.
Exact accounts, because turn always balances.

temporality.code: one-way inward drift, no stable orbit; round ~ r^2 per band; instant stir
temporality.note: The Draw makes every orbit decay inward, so aging, sinking and 'older' coincide: towns are founded at the Rim, grow rich inward and are torn apart at the Wall. A round quarters when distance halves, so each band keeps its own calendar and inner lives run hot and short. Stir acts instantly at any range. Unravelling spreads a whirl into its surroundings; the laws give no way back.

conservation.code: signed turn conserved: made/unmade only in opposite twins; death spreads it
conservation.note: Turn is never created or destroyed, only divided. Equal opposites meeting become froth, itself paired spray, which frays into still Deep; eating merges like hands, burning cancels unlike ones. A starved whirl's turn widens into its surroundings instead of vanishing, so a graveyard carries a faint net hand. The ledger can therefore close exactly: every gain has a twin somewhere, and unexplained turn is evidence of crime.

agency.code: company-only: no self-motion; pairs travel, walls carry; steering spends turn
agency.note: No whirl or braid can move its own heart by moving its parts. Alone, a person goes only where the Floor's drift carries her or one way along a wall; with an equal opposite partner she travels straight, and every corner costs a trim pellet swallowed by one partner and later matched by the other. Towns steer by the balance of turn between their halves, so trade is navigation. Power is choosing company: pairing, splitting at walls, seating a checkerboard, or forcing a merge.

identity.code: processual: a thing is its turning, not its matter; the twin pair is the unit
identity.note: The Deep passes through every whirl, so what persists is pattern, never substance; hand, turn, eye and draw describe a thing completely, and a person is a braid of whirls around one heart-eye. Every birth is a twin birth, so the pair, with mirrored names and an even bowl, is the social unit, and one whose twin has died is a half. A thing ends by unravelling, by being torn, or by merging with a like hand within three eye-widths, after which neither survives as itself.

scarcity.code: scarce: livable shear band, outward ground, keeping flow, matched partners
scarcity.note: Only the middle bands are livable: the Rim starves, the Wall tears, the Eye stills. Holding a town's band against the inward creep is the steady work of civic life. Keeping anything needs moving Deep, so tending is the largest trade, and every wall trades mirror against feed. Travel needs an equal opposite partner, hence matchers; and making one thing makes an unwanted twin that must be stored far from its partner.

information_flow.code: instant stir, any range: loners loud, pairs quiet; records live while turning
information_flow.note: Every whirl stirs the whole Deep instantly; there is no light and no contact. A loner's stir carries far, while a pair's two stirs cancel at a distance, the closer the quieter: any loner can be placed, a close pair hardly found, and the Hum of all loners swells toward the Wall. To be felt far away needs a strong lone whirl whose twin is kept far off. Records are knotted whirl-patterns that unravel when their flow stops, so archives are carousels kept turning by rote.

boundary_structure.code: walls mirror opposite hand; calm in walled checkerboards; life in mid-bands
boundary_structure.note: A solid boundary answers each nearby whirl with an opposite-handed mirror, so walls carry loners one way, split arriving pairs, sort crowds by Hand and starve the rooms they shelter; a sealed room is a small Eye. Stillness needs a checkerboard of both hands: a stone is one, and a council is one walled on its outer cell edges so the mirrors complete the pattern; one wrong seat sets the room creeping. At world scale the Rim starves, the Wall tears and the Eye stills; the Throat is a one-way exit.

permitted_transformations.code: make only in twins, merge like, burn unlike; sinking free, outward costly
permitted_transformations.note: Spinning up needs an equal opposite twin, so goods come in twin lots and counterstock must be stored apart; equal opposites meeting become froth, which burners meter into heat. Like hands within three eye-widths merge (eating, welding, growth); unlike hands cancel in part (burning). Stirring sorts heavy to the eye and loose to the rim. Sinking inward is the default; holding a band or climbing outward takes a balanced town and steady work. Too little shear spreads a whirl; too much tears it to froth.

enforcement.code: automatic, instant physical; social law mirrors the turn ledger and pairing
enforcement.note: Physics enforces itself: an unequal pair circles, a one-handed crush merges into one whirl, a sealed room starves. Social law copies the conservation: ledgerers record where every twin lies, and the gravest crime, a forced merge, shows as sudden unexplained turn. Twins share the even bowl so they can keep travelling straight together; stillness is taboo; councils need every seat correctly filled.

worlds.title: The Kept World: Where Every Change Is Someone's Gift
worlds.text:
The Kept World: Where Every Change Is Someone's Gift

1. The core principle

In the Kept World there is only one cause: a gift. A change happens only when a person gives some of their store, which is the world's single currency of change. The receiver then takes exactly the change that store paid for. Things have no natures or tendencies, only conditions. So the stillness relation is not an extra law. It is simply what happens when there is no other cause: if no one is giving to a thing, nothing can make it different, and it stays exactly as it is.

Potlatch shapes everything else. Giving is the only way to act on the world. Being given to binds you. Your power is measured by what you have given away and not yet had back.

People reason about this as calmly as we reason about a locked drawer: whatever you left is still there, exactly as you left it. Every "why did this change?" has the answer "someone paid for it", and there is always a name to find. Children learn this with their first toy. A dropped cup hangs in the air, and a toy that moved always had a mover.

2. The rules

R1 — Keeping. Whatever no one is giving to stays exactly as it is in every way: place, shape, heat, colour, freshness, tension, memory, mood and debt.
- Nothing falls, flows, cools, spreads, rots, rusts, ages, heals, fades or is forgotten on its own.
- A kettle heated a century ago is still exactly as hot. A drawn bow stays drawn forever and never looses its arrow. Spoken words hang in the air where they were said.
- A gift of motion is a gift of a journey. The giver decides where the thing goes; it goes there and stops. Nothing coasts past what was paid for, and there is no up or down.
- For anything untouched, its state now is its state at its last gift.

R2 — The Gift.
- Only people give. Everything else (stone, water, air, grain, beasts) is a thing. A thing can receive a change and keep it, but it never gives, so it can never pass a change on.
- A thrown stone that hits a window stops against it. The window breaks only if someone pays to break it. No lever, spring, wheel, fire or current does any work. Every effect is paid for directly, by the giver's own touch.
- A change costs its giver store equal to its size. One measure carries a grown person's weight a hundred paces, brings a kettle from cold to boiling-hot, or leaves about ten words hanging in the air.
- A waking hour of looking, listening and thinking costs about one measure. Seeing needs no light, because it is something the seer does.
- Store is never used up. It sits in the change it bought, and every change carries its maker's name, readable by anyone who looks closely.
- Only the maker can undo a change, and only if nobody has changed that thing since. Undoing gives the maker back the full store, so a round trip or a corrected mistake costs them nothing.
- No one can take store from a person. It leaves a person only when they give it.
- The only change one person can make to another is to give them store. Your body, place and mind change only when you spend on them, so no one can move, wound or kill anyone else.

R3 — Debt.
- When a person receives store from another person, with at least one third person watching as witness, the receiver owes the giver exactly that much.
- A gift cannot be refused. A gift given with no witness moves the store but binds no one.
- Debts never fade (R1). Only repayment, which needs no witness, or the creditor's forgiveness ends a debt.
- While you owe anyone, every measure you give to any person, witnessed or not, goes first to your creditors, oldest debt first, until you are clear. It reaches them wherever they are; debt is the one thing that travels without touch. Only what is left over reaches the person you meant.
- Spending on things or on yourself is never redirected this way.
- Between two people there is only one balance. If you return more than you owe, your debt is cleared and the other person now owes you the extra.

R4 — Standing.
- Your standing is what others currently owe you, plus everything you have broken (R5).
- Standing sets your pace, the fastest you can spend store. Everyone has 20 measures an hour, plus 1 more an hour for each measure of standing.
- Store is how much you can do; standing is how fast. Receiving makes you rich but bound. Giving makes you fast but poor. Being repaid slows you down.

R5 — Breaking.
- In front of witnesses, you may break a change you made, which means giving it up forever.
- No one can ever undo it, though others may build over it. The store in it leaves the world for good, and your standing rises by that amount permanently, owed by no one.
- Nothing adds store to the world, and breaking is the only thing that removes it. So the world's total store is fixed, except that every breaking makes it smaller.

3. How people live

Givings. Everything that matters happens at a Giving, because witnesses make gifts binding.
- The host gives to the gathered guests, and each guest watches the others receive. By the end, a hall full of people owes the host, and the host's pace has multiplied.
- The guests must hold Givings of their own. They try to give back more than they got, so that the balance tips their way.
- Rank is simply standing, and the great really are faster. A head of house owed 50,000 measures spends about 2,500 times faster than someone owed nothing, who gets around at a slow stroll.
- Monuments are broken works that no one can ever remove. Each one is a permanent record of its breaker's pace.

Fighting with gifts. No one can harm a body, so rivalry runs through store.
- You bring down a great giver by repaying them in full and then some. This drains their pace and leaves them owing you.
- Or you bury a rival in witnessed gifts, so that whatever they give anyone reaches you first.
- Custom pushes back. A Giving must include a witness the receiver invited, gifts nobody asked for are limited, and there are "quiet gifts", given with no witness, which help someone without owning them.

Family and life.
- Parents make a child by giving store into a new person. Births are always witnessed, so every child starts life owing its parents. Under the oldest-first rule, it can give to no one else until that first debt is paid. That moment, the Squaring, is coming of age.
- Children grow exactly as fast as they are given store to grow with. Adults do not age.
- No one gets hungry, because hunger would be a change nobody makes. Food is eaten for pleasure and ceremony.
- A person whose store runs out simply stops. They do not suffer or even think. They wait, perfectly kept, until someone gives to them. Death is being stilled with no one waking you.
- Elders may hold a Last Giving: they give away everything and let themselves be stilled.
- Waking someone with a witnessed gift makes them your debtor, so decent people wake the still in secret.

Work and towns.
- Carriers are the whole of transport and industry, because nothing moves unless a hand pays for it.
- People save by making things. A house is a bank that only its builder can draw on, by unmaking it.
- Listeners visit rooms where words still hang. Courts work by listening to what was said at a scene and reading the maker's name on every change there.
- Reckoners trace chains of debt and redirected payments.
- Towns are clusters of rooms left hanging wherever they were set. There is no weather, so walls are only for privacy.
- Words in a room can only be unsaid in reverse order, so polite guests clear the air before they leave, last speaker first.

4. What is easy and what is hard

Easy:
- Keeping things. Food, heat, bodies, buildings and records last forever for free, memory is perfect, and nothing needs maintenance.
- Prediction and explanation. Anything no one touches will be tomorrow exactly what it is today, and for any change you just find the name on it.
- Safety. There are no accidents, spreading fires, floods, falls, disease, ageing or violence.
- Building. Put anything anywhere and it stays, with no foundations or supports.
- Fixing your own mistakes. It costs nothing, as long as no one has built on top of them.
- Enforcing obligations. Debts are exact and permanent, and they collect themselves.
- Waiting. The still can wait for centuries unharmed.

Hard:
- Anything automatic or large. There are no machines, chain reactions or leverage, and no wind or river to harness. Every effect is paid for by hand, at the payer's pace, so great works need great standing or a crowd.
- Getting rid of things. Nothing rots, washes away or wears out. Other people's leftovers, and everything the still ever made, stay until someone pays to build over them.
- Distance. You act only by touch, and words stay where they were spoken, so every message has to be carried.
- Escaping obligation. You cannot refuse a gift, debts never fade, older creditors come first, and a rival can bind you without your consent.
- Helping without binding. It needs secrecy, and secrecy earns the helper nothing.
- Staying awake. Even thinking costs store. The poor forget their pasts to get back the store their memories hold, which buys more waking hours, and then they slide into stillness.
- Letting go. Grief, grudges and memories never fade on their own. Forgetting is a deliberate unmaking, which returns what the memory cost.
- A shrinking world. The total store never grows, and the most honoured act, breaking, makes it smaller forever.

temporality.code: inert: no unpaid change; maker undo, last first; breaking alone is final
temporality.note: Time does nothing: a kettle heated a century ago is still exactly as hot, adults do not age and the stilled wait unharmed. Every change happens at its payer's pace, 20 measures an hour plus one per measure of standing, and stops where it was paid for; nothing coasts. Any unbroken change can be undone by its maker for a full refund, but only from the top of that thing's stack of changes, so another's later work locks it. Witnessed breaking is the one change that no one can ever undo, and the world's only arrow: each one shrinks the total store for good.

conservation.code: store conserved in signed changes; undo refunds; debts exact; breaking deletes
conservation.note: Store is never used up: it sits in the change it bought, under the maker's name, or in the person it was given to, and no one can take it. Debts are exact and never fade; two people share one netted balance, so over-repayment flips its sign, and a witnessed gift makes an equal pair, the receiver's debt and the giver's claim. Unwitnessed gifts move store without binding. Breaking is the only sink: it removes a change's store from the world and turns it into permanent standing owed by no one.

agency.code: gift-only: persons alone cause, by paid touch; power = given, not yet repaid
agency.note: Only persons give. Things receive and keep a change but never pass it on, so no lever, spring, fire or current works and every effect is paid by the giver's own touch. No one can move, wound or kill another; the only act on a person is giving them store, which cannot be refused.
